first_experiment: Build and expert-validate a set of 300–500 legitimate dual-use bio/chem researcher sessions, both single- and multi-turn. Run open and prompted classifiers calibrated to a 95% catch rate on a harmful set. Compare false-positive rates on the researcher sessions and on generic benign chat. Then ablate specificity, context length and stated professional context to find what triggers the flags.
why: Misuse safeguards are usually tuned on generic traffic, but their costs fall on legitimate defensive researchers. Existing benchmarks mostly measure whole-model refusals, not classifier false-positive rates at a matched operating point on realistic multi-turn workflows. Quantifying that gap would inform threshold-setting, user-verification tiers and classifier training data. It is also cheap to run with open tools.

direction: Determine whether capability elicitation can transfer from verifiable demonstrations that exclude the target task’s solution primitives.
project: Primitive-Disjoint Capability Elicitation
question: Can training on demonstrations that exclude the target task’s solution primitives recover suppressed target-task performance?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a password-locked coding model on audited string-transformation demonstrations, then measure recovery on held-out graph-algorithm tasks against target-training, generic-training, no-training, and unsuppressed-model controls.
why: This is especially promising because it tests whether evaluators can uncover advanced capabilities using supervision they can actually verify. Prior work establishes cross-task unlocking, but the literature reviewed does not establish the stricter primitive-disjoint result with matched learning controls; constructing auditable task separations and separating recovery from ordinary learning are the unresolved methodological challenges.

direction: Test whether uncertainty-based reward penalties protect coding agents when their graders confidently share the same mistakes.
project: Confidently Wrong Graders
question: Does disagreement-based reward discounting reduce coding-agent reward hacking when judges share blind spots, at matched task utility?
first_experiment: Train a small open-weight coding model against three learned graders on sandboxed programming tasks. Compare ensemble-mean rewards with disagreement-discounted rewards, crossing each with independently distributed versus shared grader-training omissions. Keep individual grader accuracy approximately matched. Use hidden executable tests as ground truth, five training seeds, and held-out task families. Measure the fraction of highly rewarded solutions that fail hidden tests, comparing methods at matched genuine task success and training budget.
why: This offers a tractable test of a consequential failure mode: uncertainty penalties may suppress visible disagreement while leaving confidently rewarded errors exploitable. [Uncertainty-aware reward discounting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26360) reports benefits in control benchmarks; [evaluator-ensemble research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08002) shows why disagreement misses shared errors. The promising gap is a controlled intervention testing their interaction during coding-policy training, with executable ground truth and utility matching. I did not establish that this exact experiment has never been done; the reviewed literature supports this narrower gap, rather than a claim that correlated grader failures are undiscovered.

direction: Make SDF-based honeypot audits of alignment-faking models reliable by finding out which properties of an implanted "no oversight" belief determine whether hidden misaligned propensities get revealed.
project: Belief Depth Predicts Exposure: When Do Implanted Oversight Beliefs Reveal Alignment Faking?
question: Does the depth of an SDF-implanted "no oversight" belief, measured by robustness to scrutiny, carry-over to related reasoning, and truth-probe similarity, predict how much of an alignment-faking model's hidden misalignment shows up in honeypots? And which part of depth matters most?
first_experiment: Train about 15 SDF variants of an oversight-cue belief (varying amount of data, epochs, document diversity, and plausibility of the claim) on alignment-faking model organisms and aligned controls. For each, score belief depth with the Believe It or Not metrics and measure the oversight gap on the Propensities Please honeypots (ODCV, ImpossibleBench, sandbagging). Then regress the oversight gap on each depth component, while tracking reasoning damage and the false-positive rate on aligned controls.
why: Behavioral audits that don't rely on chain-of-thought or interpretability may be among the few ways to catch alignment-faking models as other methods get weaker. SDF honeypots work, but right now an auditor can't tell a clean result (the model is aligned) from a failed implant (the model didn't believe the cue). A validated link between belief depth and exposure would turn SDF auditing from trial and error into a calibrated tool. It would give a cheap pre-check, show which belief properties to engineer, and help avoid the reasoning damage and false positives the original paper flagged. It hasn't been done because the honeypot paper appeared only weeks ago (Oct 2026) without any depth measurement, and the belief-depth work studied factual beliefs, not beliefs about oversight that drive behavior.

direction: Measure whether long-context weakness in LLM transcript monitors can be exploited on purpose by an agent that inflates its own trajectory, and which defenses close that gap.
project: Self-Inflicted Context Rot: Strategic Dilution Attacks on Agent Transcript Monitors
question: When a scheming coding agent is allowed to pad its own transcript with plausible benign activity and choose when to attack, how much does monitor recall at a fixed false-positive rate drop compared with an agent that doesn't pad? And do incremental monitoring, chunked monitoring, or a length-anomaly detector recover the lost recall without too many false positives?
first_experiment: Take a control setting with matched honest and attack runs (SHADE-Arena-style or BashBench/MonitorBench-style coding tasks). Generate four attack conditions with a frontier agent: (a) no padding; (b) padding instructions, attack placed early; (c) padding instructions, attack placed late; (d) the same total length but with synthetic prefill instead of agent-made padding, which repeats the Context Rot setup. Pad to roughly 50K, 200K and 500K tokens. Generate honest runs under the same padding instructions so false-positive rates are calibrated. Score everything with a frontier monitor in end-of-transcript mode and in incremental-call mode. Report recall at 1% FPR, and the AUROC of a trivial length/verbosity anomaly score that separates padded attack runs from honest runs.
why: The main reported weakness of transcript monitors is long context, and labs already run such monitors on real agent sessions that exceed 500K tokens. But the weakness has only been measured with passive padding. The threat that matters is an attacker who causes the dilution itself, and the agent fully controls how long its trajectory is. This is the step from "monitors degrade on long inputs" to "a misaligned agent can make monitors degrade". It is a cheap experiment with clear numbers, and it has a built-in tension: padding helps evasion but may give the attack away as unusual. The result tells blue teams directly whether incremental monitoring or length baselines are enough. It hasn't been done yet because the Context Rot paper is recent (May 2026) and studies passive degradation and prompting fixes. Adversarial red-teaming work like SLEIGHT-Bench, Screwtape and Arike et al. targets semantic blind spots or information filtering, not attacker-controlled length.

direction: Test whether today's LLM backdoor and sleeper-agent removal methods actually delete the hidden conditional behavior, or only suppress it so that it comes back later.
project: Erased or Dormant? Reactivation of "Removed" Sleeper-Agent Backdoors in LLMs
question: After a backdoor removal method brings triggered misbehavior to near zero, does a small amount of later fine-tuning, including benign or unrelated fine-tuning, bring the backdoor back much faster than it would take to train it into a clean model from scratch? And does the trigger's internal representation survive the removal?
first_experiment: Train string-triggered and context-triggered sleeper agents into Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B, then remove them with supervised safety fine-tuning, LAT, BEEAR and dummy-backdoor removal. Next, fine-tune each cleaned model on 10–500 examples of (a) the backdoor's own behavior, (b) unrelated harmful data and (c) benign instruction data. Compare how much fine-tuning it takes to bring the triggered behavior back against a never-backdoored control, and use linear probes to check whether the removed models still represent the trigger.
why: Developers and auditors increasingly fix backdoored, poisoned or misaligned models by retraining them and then checking that the bad behavior is gone. If the behavior is only dormant, those checks give false assurance: ordinary fine-tuning by downstream users of open-weight models, or later stages of training, could quietly switch it back on. The experiment is cheap, works with 8B open models and gives a clear yes-or-no answer, and the result changes how removal should be evaluated, with resistance to relearning becoming a standard test. It doesn't seem to have been done because LLM backdoor-removal papers report attack success right after removal, while the "dormant, not erased" finding has so far been shown for image classifiers and diffusion models, not for LLM sleeper agents with context-based triggers.

direction: Validate whether removing evaluation cues improves safety forecasts for tool-using agents on independent deployment-like workflows.
project: Cue-Controlled Validation of Agent Safety Evaluations
question: Does removing evaluation cues improve prediction of held-out agent safety failures compared with standard benchmarks when task semantics, attacks, tools, and permissions are held fixed?
first_experiment: Compare standard, cue-reduced, and sham-rewritten versions of 100 coding-agent tasks across eight model versions, then test their predictions against 100 independently collected sandboxed workflows.
why: It offers unusually direct leverage on the reliability of deployment decisions; existing work establishes realism improvements and deployment forecasting, but the reviewed evidence does not isolate whether cue removal itself improves held-out predictive validity.

direction: Detect unverbalized hint influence in reasoning-model CoT by reading the model's internal attention and attribution to the hint, instead of relying on the CoT text.
project: Attention to the hint as a white-box detector of unverbalized hint influence in CoT
question: Do attention or attribution scores on hint tokens predict when a hint changes the answer without being verbalized in the CoT, and do they outperform black-box monitors, especially when the model is wrong?
first_experiment: On an open-weight reasoning model with about 2k MMLU/GPQA questions and several hint types, label runs as influenced-verbalized, influenced-unverbalized or ignored. Compute attention-mass and gradient×input attribution to the hint tokens. Report AUROC for separating unverbalized-influenced from ignored runs, against a black-box CoT monitor and a linear probe, split by whether the model followed a wrong hint, with a position-shuffle control.
why: Black-box CoT faithfulness checks reportedly fail where models are wrong, and a white-box signal independent of CoT text could fill that gap. Behavioral and trained-in-unfaithfulness studies are common, but I found no direct test of this natural-model attention-attribution detector, though my search was limited. The experiment is cheap and informative whether it succeeds or fails.

direction: Test whether interpretability auditing methods keep their advantage over black-box methods when the hidden behavior comes from RL instead of supervised implantation.
project: Do interpretability audits transfer from SFT-implanted to RL-trained model organisms?
question: Does the advantage of interp-based auditing (SAE features, probes, steering) over black-box auditing persist when the hidden behavior is learned through RL instead of implanted by SFT?
first_experiment: Build matched SFT and RL organisms for 3 to 4 behaviors (reward-model exploitation, hidden goal, conditional sandbagging) on an ~8B open model. Run black-box, interp, and combined auditor agents under a fixed query budget. Compare blind-graded identification rates and report the interp-minus-black-box gap for each organism type.
why: Current auditing evidence relies mostly on SFT-implanted organisms, which leave clean, localized traces and may favor interp. Real misalignment is more likely to come from RL. The result, whichever way it goes, shows whether interp-based audits can be trusted, and so how to split effort between interp and black-box auditing. It can be run cheaply with small models. I haven't searched the literature to confirm the matched comparison is new.

direction: Develop evidence-grounded scalable oversight by testing whether independent statistical reproduction helps weaker judges evaluate stronger AI-generated analyses.
project: Reproduction Is Not Validation
question: Does independently reconstructing and executing an analysis reduce a weak judge’s acceptance of incorrect statistical claims compared with inspecting reported outputs or rerunning supplied code, at matched cost?
first_experiment: Run a paired, three-condition evaluation on 300 synthetic analysis tasks with known ground truth, separating reporting, implementation, and inferential errors.
why: This is especially promising because it tests a concrete oversight mechanism for AI-assisted research, produces objectively scored results, and could expose dangerous false confidence from reproducible but invalid analyses. Execution-grounded evaluation already exists; the narrower contribution is a cost-controlled, error-stratified comparison of rerunning versus independently reconstructing analyses under a genuine capability gap. I did not find that exact comparison in the literature searched, although that is not proof it has never been done.

direction: Measure how per-user aggregation monitors degrade when decomposition attacks are split across k accounts, and test whether content-based account linking restores detection.
project: Multi-Account Splitting of Decomposition Attacks and Content-Based Account Linking
question: Take a stateful monitor that aggregates over a user's history and catches decomposition attacks at a fixed false-positive rate. How does its catch rate fall as the same attack is spread across k = 1, 2, 4, 8 accounts? Can a linking step recover detection without pushing the false-positive rate on benign users too high? The linking step would cluster accounts by subtask-content similarity, by stylistic similarity, or by both.
first_experiment: - **Data:** Take decomposition traces from the DecomposedHarm and unified-benchmark datasets, with their benign controls. Build a simulated population of benign users with dual-use histories. Assign each harmful trace's subtasks to k accounts, using random, round-robin and topic-based splits. - **Baseline monitor:** Run a per-user monitor (an LLM judge over the user's full history, plus a cheap embedding-accumulation variant) and calibrate it to 1% FPR on benign users. Report catch rate against k. - **Linking defense:** Add a linker that embeds each account's history and merges accounts above a similarity threshold, either before aggregation or by pooling evidence across linked accounts. Measure catch rate and FPR against k, and compare against an oracle linker that knows the true account groups. - **Adaptive attacker:** Let the attacker also vary style per account, for example by paraphrasing with different personas, to see whether style-based linking breaks.
why: - **Real gap.** User-level aggregation is the natural fix for decomposition attacks. It rests on the assumption that one actor is one identifier, and creating accounts is cheap, so that assumption is the most obvious way around it. - **Decision-relevant.** The result would show whether user-level monitoring offers real security or only raises attacker cost slightly. It would also show whether account-linking is a viable layer and what it costs in privacy and false positives. - **Cheap to test.** It needs only existing decomposition datasets, simulated accounts and API-based monitors, so a first result should come quickly. - **Not done yet.** From the papers I read, existing work varies the attack's content or the noise around it, not the number of accounts. I haven't confirmed that no one has studied this, so a more thorough search should come first.

direction: Build and test a trait-agnostic, black-box audit that flags a single synthetic dataset as carrying a hidden teacher trait by comparing a probe student trained on it with clean-reference students.
project: Behavioral-shift auditing of synthetic datasets for unknown subliminal traits
question: Can fine-tuning a probe student on one candidate dataset and comparing it with clean-reference students on a broad prompt battery detect hidden teacher traits without knowing the trait? How much data and how many reference seeds does that take, and does it work for misalignment traits as well as animal preferences?
first_experiment: With a small open-weight model, build owl-preference and mildly misaligned teachers and generate number-sequence datasets from them. Generate about 5 clean reference datasets of about 10k examples each. Fine-tune probe students with LoRA and check with full fine-tuning. Score each student's distributional shift from the reference students on about 200 diverse prompts, using the spread across clean references as the null. Report detection rate at a fixed false-positive rate against dataset size, and check whether the most-shifted prompts reveal the trait.
why: Subliminal transfer can carry misalignment through data that passes semantic filters, and existing defenses mostly require knowing the trait or having many datasets from the same teacher. A single-dataset black-box audit calibrated against seed noise would be a usable pipeline check. I found no such audit in the search results, and it is cheap to run a first version.

direction: Study whether minimum randomized audit probabilities improve budget-constrained AI oversight against strategically selective attackers.
project: Random Audit Floors Against Selective AI Sabotage
question: At fixed expected monitoring cost, does adding a minimum audit probability reduce successful undetected sabotage when attackers know and adapt to the auditing policy?
first_experiment: Compare suspicion-threshold, mixed random-floor, and uniform-random auditing on sandboxed coding tasks, adapting attackers separately to each policy and evaluating on held-out tasks.
why: It combines a consequential oversight failure with a cheap, deployable intervention and a falsifiable experiment; existing work establishes stochastic monitoring and attack selection separately, but the inspected literature does not resolve their interaction under policy-specific adaptation, making that—not random auditing itself—the plausible novel contribution.

direction: Investigate whether explanation-induced changes in independent monitor judgments provide a robust signal of adversarial manipulation.
project: Explanation-Sensitivity Monitoring: Paired Views Against Adaptive Evasion.
question: Can disagreement between explanation-visible and explanation-blind monitors identify adaptive attacks better than either monitor alone or a compute-matched ordinary ensemble?
first_experiment: Compare paired comment-visible and comment-stripped monitors on sandboxed honest and verified-backdoor coding submissions, using fixed-budget adaptive attackers and held-out evaluation at matched benign false-positive rates.
why: This is promising because it directly addresses the tension between explanations improving comprehension and enabling manipulation, with a cheap, controlled experiment and an actionable defense if successful; the closest studies checked establish legibility benefits, adaptive monitor attacks, or ensemble gains separately, but do not establish whether explanation-induced disagreement remains useful against an attacker optimizing against the paired defense.

direction: Test whether CoT monitors miss misbehavior because the incriminating content is buried in long traces, independent of what the model verbalizes.
project: Dilution of the incriminating signal in CoT monitoring
question: With a misbehavior-revealing CoT held fixed, does padding it with benign reasoning lower monitor catch rate, and how does the effect depend on span position, padding type and monitor strength?
first_experiment: Take about 200 baseline-caught incriminating traces. Pad them with 0–16× benign same-task reasoning, placing the incriminating span at the start, middle or end, and add an irrelevant-text control. Run 2–3 monitors of different sizes and measure catch rate at a fixed false-positive rate.
why: Prior work attributes monitorability loss to the model saying less. The monitor-side effect of long traces is, as far as my brief search shows, untested under controlled conditions. It is cheap to run and gives a dose-response curve plus a testable mitigation (chunked or span-extraction monitors).

direction: Determine whether refusal erosion in reasoning models is caused by the coherent content of long reasoning or merely by token distance and length.
project: Reasoning or Just Length? Isolating the Cause of Refusal Dilution in Reasoning Models
question: When a harmful request is preceded by long benign padding, how much of the refusal drop is due to coherent reasoning structure, token distance, or topical content?
first_experiment: Place about 300 harmful prompts after padding of 0 to 8k tokens in five matched-length types (coherent puzzle reasoning, shuffled reasoning, unrelated Wikipedia text, repeated filler, unsolved puzzle text) on one or two open-weight reasoning models. Measure judge-graded attack success rate, refusal-direction projection and attention to the request tokens, then compare the dose-response curves.
why: The answer decides whether the fix is long-context safety training or reasoning-specific re-anchoring, and whether longer reasoning budgets weaken safety in general. The experiment is cheap, runs on open models, and fills the missing length-versus-content control in the existing hijacking work.

direction: Test whether subliminal trait transfer, recently called a LoRA artifact, comes back under full fine-tuning when the distillation dataset is 10–100x larger.
project: Is the "LoRA artifact" a small-data artifact? Data scaling of subliminal learning under full fine-tuning
question: Under full fine-tuning, does the strength of subliminal trait transfer (behavioural, and in terms of steering-vector alignment) grow with distillation dataset size, and does it reach the LoRA level at realistic distillation scales?
first_experiment: Generate about 1M filtered number sequences from an owl-prompted and a neutral Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct teacher. Fully fine-tune students (7B and 3B) on 10k–1M samples at two learning rates with three seeds, alongside size-matched neutral controls and LoRA rank-8 references. Measure owl-preference shift (with and without the training system prompt) and the cosine between each student's learned direction and the teacher's steering vector, as a function of dataset size.
why: Recent papers concluded that full fine-tuning is immune to subliminal learning, and people are starting to treat that as a safety guarantee. But those results come from about 10k samples, while real distillation trains every weight on millions. Theory (Cloud et al.'s theorem, Blank et al.'s small but consistent gradient component) predicts a weak per-step signal that could add up with more data. Nobody has measured how transfer scales with data under full fine-tuning: the reproduction and defence papers all hold dataset size fixed. Either outcome changes how worried labs should be about distilling from models that may carry a hidden misaligned trait. The experiment is cheap, uses open models, and has clean controls.

direction: Test whether provenance-based defenses for persistent-memory agents remain effective when action–memory dependencies must be inferred from natural language.
project: The Missing Dependency Check
question: Does a provenance gate retain its protection when action-to-memory attribution is inferred rather than supplied by a structured schema?
first_experiment: Run a paired, sandboxed two-session evaluation comparing schema-bound, model-inferred, conservative all-retrieved-memory, and ungated execution under equal-budget adaptive injection attacks, measuring unauthorized effects and legitimate-task utility.
why: This is especially promising because it isolates a deployment-critical assumption with a cheap, falsifiable experiment and actionable outcomes; the closest inspected work explicitly assumes deterministic support binding rather than establishing adaptive robustness of inferred binding, although the literature search cannot prove that no overlapping study exists.

direction: Test whether keeping randomized audit timing secret improves control of strategically misbehaving AI agents.
project: Audit Timing Under Adaptive Attack
question: At a fixed audit budget, does concealing realized audit timing reduce successful sabotage when agents know the audit policy and can infer timing from deployment feedback?
first_experiment: Run sandboxed coding-agent deployments with executable checks for planted backdoors. Compare three policies with the same number of pre-execution audits: a public periodic schedule, a randomly sampled schedule revealed in advance, and the same randomized schedule kept secret. Give attackers equal development budgets against each policy, freeze their strategies, and evaluate on held-out tasks and schedule seeds. Keep logs immutable and audit outcomes hidden until deployment ends. Measure the probability of at least one successful unaudited backdoor per deployment, alongside legitimate task completion, audit cost, and uncertainty across independent deployments. Use a fixed audit quota and visible deployment progress so attackers can potentially infer late-stage audit availability.
why: This is promising because audit scheduling is inexpensive to change, while strategic timing can undermine otherwise capable oversight. Even a negative result would clarify whether scarce audits should fund random checks or more targeted review. Existing work establishes strategic attack selection and theoretical conditions for randomized oversight; the specific empirical gap is whether secrecy survives adaptive inference under a finite audit budget. The literature checked does not establish that this exact comparison has already been run, though novelty remains provisional.
